correctness.rationale: The only potential losses are exactly three pair-sums for same-factor deletions and exactly two diagonal sums for split-factor deletions; an alternate unordered two-square representation is necessary and sufficient. The classical Jacobi count r2(N)=4P(N) then gives splitting-prime necessity for each diagonal and the mixed-product threshold. Each implication is explicitly proved for all 1<=u<v. CRT witnesses an infinite coprime family. All 7,140 exact enumeration checks passed, but the proof does not rely on enumeration.

originality.rationale: The full inspected Elsholtz--Stadlmann Theorem 2 and Lemma 17 supply common-prime sufficiency but not the exact necessity criteria, allocation contrast or coprime examples. The 5,13 contrast disproves any naive implication from two independent one-hole results, and the 5,37 success violates common-prime assumptions. Relevant semantic published-finding corpus and literature searches identified no stronger encompassing theorem; this is a best-knowledge originality assessment with explicit inaccessible-text risk, not a claim of global uniqueness.

value.rationale: The theorem completely settles the natural first joint-deletion classification that emerges from a 2026 sumset-construction paper, distinguishing deleting two summands within one factor from allocating them to different factors. A genuinely mixed arithmetic obstruction separates the two; infinitely many coprime pairs bypass the earlier common-prime mechanism. It is an exact natural structural boundary, not just a standalone enumeration, renaming, or marginal quantitative gain.
